title: Service without an audience
hook: seva is service done with no reward in mind, and it is meant to change the one who serves

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp two closed with jot, the one light in all ten Gurus. Your line was one light, ten lamps. Did you tell someone about the light you saw in them? Day ninety-seven.

Welcome to camp three. For seventy-five days you heard the stories. Now, for the next stretch of the path, you try the practices, one at a time, starting with the one Sikhs put first. Here's a small test. The last time you did something good for someone, did you tell anyone? A post, a mention at dinner, a little hint so they'd know it was you? That pull is human. A kindness can feel half finished until someone sees it. Now, a snowy street at six in the morning. One neighbor's walk is already shoveled. Nobody saw who did it. Nobody ever will. That's today's word.
screen: `CAMP THREE: THE PRACTICES.` → `DID YOU TELL ANYONE?` → `THE WALK SHOVELED AT SIX.`

segments.voice: Nishkam seva. Seva you already know from day one: service. Nishkam means without desire. Nish, without; kam, wanting. Service with nothing wanted back. No thanks, no credit, no reward, not even the good feeling of being seen as a good person. The Gurus put it at the heart of Sikh life. In the Sukhmani, the long hymn of peace by Guru Arjan, there's a line on it. In paraphrase, it says that whoever serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord. And Guru Nanak says it from the other side: serve in this world, and you will find a seat in the court of the divine. Here's the surprising part. Seva isn't mainly about the person you help. Of course they matter; the hungry get fed. But the Gurus say seva works on the one who serves. Sikhs say each good thing left unseen starves a little of the self that wants attention. Sikhs call that self haumai, and we'll give it a whole day later this week. So seva is practice, like a scale on a piano. It's how the teaching gets out of your head and into your hands. That's why it opens camp three. In the gurdwara you'll see it everywhere: people chopping onions, wiping tables, washing pots, and nobody announces who they are. A doctor, a student, a grandmother, all with their sleeves rolled up. The rule is simple. Do the good thing. Then walk away.
screen: `NISHKAM — WITHOUT WANTING.` · `SERVE, AND FIND A SEAT.` · `SEVA CHANGES THE ONE WHO SERVES.` · `SLEEVES UP, NAMES OFF.` · then, large: `NO ONE NEEDS TO KNOW.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let your breathing slow. Think of one small, unseen kindness you could do today. Refilling the coffee filter at work. Taking a neighbor's bin in. Paying a small bill someone won't notice. Picture yourself doing it. Now picture walking away without saying a word. Notice the little itch to be known. You don't have to fight it. Just see it, and smile at it. Then choose your kindness. The bell holds the time.
Nishkam seva. Selfless service: help given with nothing wanted back, which changes the one who gives it.
Your line: no one needs to know. Today, do the unseen kindness you chose, and tell no one, not even tomorrow. Day ninety-seven.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, Sikhs of every background do seva side by side, cooking, cleaning and serving, and many try to do it quietly, without asking for thanks or recognition.

fork.reveal: nishkam seva is service with nothing wanted back, not even thanks. the Gurus say that's where it does its work.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: service without desire for reward.

trapdoor: what it means: service done with nothing wanted back, which the Gurus say changes the one who serves.
what a scholar hears: Sukhmani (Ang 286) promises the Lord to one who serves without desire; Guru Nanak (Ang 26) links seva in this world to a seat in the divine court.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286 (Sukhmani, Guru Arjan: one who serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26 (Guru Nanak, Sri Raag: serve in this world and find a seat in the divine court)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook rewritten to drop 'Think about... Now picture' and the 'most of us do' claim; removed 'a line Sikhs quote often' (unsourced); the claim that unseen kindness starves the ego is now attributed to Sikhs, not stated by the narrator.
Ang 286 (seva karat hoi nihkami, tis kau hot prapat suami) paraphrased; confirm Ang.
Ang 26 (vich dunia sev kamaiai ta dargah baisan paiai) paraphrased; confirm Ang and attribution to Guru Nanak.
Nishkam etymology (nish-, without; kam, desire) simplified; confirm.
